title: GATE CS 2002
instructions: Verified selected scan: GATE 2002, Computer Science & Engineering; single paper with no set/session label. The visible header is 2002 even though the defective text layer reads 2001. Physical filename 2002.pdf is preserved.

Section A: Q1-25 are one-mark MCQs and Q26-50 are two-mark MCQs. Section B: Q51-70 are five-mark written questions; answer ANY FIFTEEN. Maximum 150 marks; 175 marks of questions are available. No General Aptitude section belongs to this paper.
The supplied ten-page scan does not state duration or negative marking. Practice settings are 180 minutes and zero MCQ penalty; these are not claimed as verified official 2002 rules.

All 70 positions have authored worked references. No official 2002 answer key was located. Supplied Made Easy keys and selected GATE Overflow discussions were cross-checked; per-question provenance states the actual scope. Historical labels 1.1-1.25, 2.1-2.25 and 3-22 are retained alongside source positions 1-70.

Q37, Q39, Q46 and Q50 are disputed or ambiguous single-choice items (8 marks) and require post-submission self-assessment. The other 46 MCQs have 67 automatically gradable marks. Source option defects and interpretation assumptions are documented in the worked references.

Written responses autosave; the server enforces the limit of 15 nonempty Section B responses. Compare submitted responses with the worked references and save clearly labeled self-assessed marks. Q60, Q63 and Q65 include explicit interpretation policies.

questions.text: The solution to the recurrence equation $T(2^k) = 3T(2^{k-1}) + 1, T(1) = 1$ is
questions.subject: 1. Discrete Maths
questions.referenceAnswer: Put $S_k=T(2^k)$. Iteration gives $S_k=3^k+\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}3^j=(3^{k+1}-1)/2$, satisfying $S_0=1$.

questions.text: Which of the following is true?
questions.optA: The set of all rational negative numbers forms a group under multiplication.
questions.optB: The set of all non-singular matrices forms a group under multiplication.
questions.optC: The set of all matrices forms a group under multiplication.

questions.subject: 2. TOC

questions.text: "If X then Y unless Z" is represented by which of the following formulas in propositional logic? ("$\neg$" is negation, "$\wedge$" is conjunction, and "$\rightarrow$" is implication)
questions.subject: 1. Discrete Maths
questions.referenceAnswer: Unless Z means when Z is false. Thus the obligation is $X\land\neg Z\Rightarrow Y$, equivalently $X\Rightarrow(Y\lor Z)$.

questions.text: In the C language
questions.optA: at most one activation record exists between the current activation record and the activation record for the main

Consider the following logic circuit whose inputs are functions $f_1,f_2,f_3$ and output is $f$. Given that
[IMG_1]
$$f_1(x,y,z)=\Sigma(0,1,3,5),\quad f_2(x,y,z)=\Sigma(6,7),\quad f(x,y,z)=\Sigma(1,4,5),$$

questions.text:
Consider the following algorithm for searching for a given number $x$ in an unsorted array $A[1\ldots n]$ having $n$ distinct values:
[CODE]
Assuming that $x$ is present on $A$, what is the expected number of comparisons made by the algorithm before it terminates?
questions.code:
1. Choose an i uniformly at random from 1...n;
2. If A[i] = x then Stop else Goto 1;
questions.subject: 7. Algorithms
questions.referenceAnswer: Each independent random probe succeeds with probability $1/n$. With replacement the number of probes is geometric, giving expectation $n$. It is not a permutation scan.

questions.text:
Let A be a set of $n>0$ elements. Let $N_r$ be the number of binary relations on A and let $N_f$ be the number of functions from A to A.
(a) Give the expression for $N_r$ in terms of n.
(b) Give the expression for $N_f$ in terms of n.
(c) Which is larger for all n, $N_r$ or $N_f$?
questions.referenceAnswer: (a) $N_r=2^{n^2}$, since a relation is any subset of $A\times A$. (b) $N_f=n^n$, since each argument independently chooses one of n images. (c) $2^n>n$ for all integers $n\geq1$, so $(2^n)^n>n^n$: $N_r>N_f$.

Assume the clock period is greater than the settling time of all circuits.

questions.text:
Consider the following 32-bit floating-point representation. There are three fields: a one-bit sign (0 positive, 1 negative), a 24-bit fraction with binary point at its left end, and a seven-bit exponent in excess-64 representation. The exponentiation base is 16; the sign is the most significant bit.
$$\underbrace{\text{sign}}_{1\text{ bit}}\quad\underbrace{\text{fraction}}_{24\text{ bits}}\quad\underbrace{\text{exponent}}_{7\text{ bits}}$$
(a) Represent decimal -7.5 as a normalized number in this format. Derive the fields and express the final answer in hexadecimal.
(b) What is the largest representable value? Express it as the nearest power of 10.
questions.referenceAnswer: (a) $-7.5=-0.01111_2\times16^1$. The sign is 1, fraction is 011110000000000000000000 (hex 780000), and stored exponent is 65=1000001. Concatenating these 1+24+7 bits gives hex BC000041. Normalization is in base 16: the first hexadecimal fraction digit is nonzero; there is no implicit leading bit. (b) The maximum is $(1-2^{-24})16^{127-64}=(1-2^{-24})2^{252}\approx7.2370051\times10^{75}$. The nearest order-of-magnitude power on a logarithmic scale is $10^{76}$; this states the usual meaning of nearest power.

questions.text:
In a C program an array is declared as float A[2048]. Each element is 4 bytes and the starting address is 0x00000000. The program runs on a computer with a direct-mapped data cache of size 8 Kbytes and block (line) size 16 bytes.
(a) Which elements of the array conflict with A[0] in the data cache? Justify briefly.
(b) If the program accesses the elements one by one in reverse order, from last to first, how many data-cache misses occur? Justify briefly. Assume the cache is initially empty and no other data or instruction accesses are considered.
questions.referenceAnswer: The array occupies exactly $2048\cdot4=8192$ bytes and the cache has $8192/16=512$ lines. (a) A[0] through A[3] share block 0 and do not conflict with one another; every other array block maps to a different line. Thus no other block within this array conflicts with A[0]. A[2048] would start the next conflicting block but is outside the array. (b) Each block incurs one compulsory miss, followed by three hits: $2048/4=512$ misses. Reverse traversal does not alter that count.

questions.text:
A university placement centre maintains the following database of companies that interview students on campus and make job offers to successful candidates. Underlined attributes are keys.
$$\begin{array}{ll}\mathrm{COMPANY}&(\underline{\mathrm{cname}},\mathrm{clocation})\\\mathrm{STUDENT}&(\underline{\mathrm{srollno}},\mathrm{sname},\mathrm{sdegree})\\\mathrm{INTERVIEW}&(\underline{\mathrm{cname},\mathrm{srollno}},\mathrm{idate})\\\mathrm{OFFER}&(\underline{\mathrm{cname},\mathrm{srollno}},\mathrm{osalary})\end{array}$$
COMPANY gives company name and location; STUDENT gives roll number, name and registered degree; INTERVIEW gives the date a company interviews a student; OFFER gives the salary offered after a successful interview.
(a) Using only relational algebra operators $\sigma,\pi,\cup,-,\times$, write queries for:
(i) Roll numbers and names of students who attended at least one interview but received no job offer.
(ii) Roll numbers and names of students who attended interviews and received offers from every company with which they interviewed.
(b) Write an SQL query listing, for each degree program in which more than five students were offered jobs, the degree name and the average offered salary of students in that degree program.
questions.referenceAnswer: Let I=projection(cname,srollno)(INTERVIEW), O=projection(cname,srollno)(OFFER), U=projection(srollno)(I), and Bad=projection(srollno)(I-O). (a)(i) T=U-projection(srollno)(O). (ii) T=U-Bad. For each part output projection(STUDENT.srollno,sname)(selection(STUDENT.srollno=T.srollno)(STUDENT cross T)); this uses only the allowed operations and excludes students without interviews. (b) SELECT s.sdegree, AVG(o.osalary) FROM STUDENT s JOIN OFFER o ON s.srollno=o.srollno GROUP BY s.sdegree HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT s.srollno)>5. This averages offers, counting each offered salary once, while counting students distinctly. If the intended average gives each student equal weight despite multiple offers, first group offers by student to compute AVG(osalary), then average those per-student values by degree; both interpretations must be stated.

questions.text:
For relation $R=(L,M,N,O,P)$, the dependencies are $M\to O$, $NO\to P$, $P\to L$, and $L\to MN$. R is decomposed into $R_1=(L,M,N,P)$ and $R_2=(M,O)$.
(a) Is this a lossless-join decomposition? Explain.
(b) Is it dependency-preserving? If not, list all the given dependencies that are not preserved.
(c) What is the highest normal form satisfied by the decomposition?
questions.referenceAnswer: (a) Yes. The intersection is M and $M\to MO=R_2$, satisfying the binary lossless-join criterion. (b) No. $NO\to P$ is not implied by the union of the projected dependencies. All other given dependencies are preserved. In particular the closure of NO under the projected union does not acquire M or P. (c) Both components are BCNF. In R1 the candidate keys are L, P and MN, and every nontrivial determinant is a superkey; $MN\to P$ follows through M to O and NO to P before projection. In R2 M is a key. Project full dependency closures, rather than simply discarding dependencies mentioning O.

questions.text:
Answer the following:
(a) The table refers to search times for a key in B-trees and B+ trees:
$$\begin{array}{c|cc}&\text{Successful}&\text{Unsuccessful}\\\text{B-tree}&X_1&X_2\\\text{B+ tree}&X_3&X_4\end{array}$$
A successful search means the key exists in the database; unsuccessful means it does not. Each entry is Constant (same search time independent of key) or Variable (dependent on the key). Give X1, X2, X3, X4.
(b) Relation R(A,B) has the following view:
[CODE]
(i) For the current R below, give V.
$$\begin{array}{c|c}A&B\\1&2\\2&3\\2&4\\4&5\\6&7\\6&8\\9&10\end{array}$$
(ii) Tuples (2,11) and (11,6) are inserted into R. What additional tuples are inserted into V?
questions.code:
CREATE VIEW V AS
(SELECT R1.A, R2.B
 FROM R AS R1, R AS R2
 WHERE R1.B = R2.A)
questions.referenceAnswer: (a) Under the conventional equal-height, node-access cost model, X1=Variable and X2=Constant. For B+ membership searches that stop at an internal separator known to represent a live key, X3=Variable and X4=Constant, as in the reviewed discussion. For ordinary record lookup (or separators retained after deletion) the search must reach a leaf, giving X3=Constant instead. The question does not specify this implementation policy or within-node comparison costs; accept a justified interpretation. (b)(i) V={(1,3),(1,4),(2,5)}. (ii) New tuples are (1,11),(2,6),(11,7),(11,8). They correspond to all newly created paths of exactly two edges, not transitive closure.

questions.text:
Answer the following:
(a) Draw the process-state transition diagram of an OS in which each process is in one of five states: created, ready, running, blocked (sleep/wait), or terminated; only non-preemptive scheduling is used. Label transitions.
(b) Atomic TEST-AND-SET is specified by the C-style pseudocode below.
[CODE]
(i) Complete enter-cs and leave-cs.
(ii) Is this critical-section solution deadlock-free and starvation-free?
(iii) Give an example showing mutual exclusion can fail if TEST-AND-SET is not atomic.
questions.rawTopic: Process Management-I (Introduction, Process, Threads & CPU Scheduling)
questions.subject: 5. Operating Systems
questions.referenceAnswer: (a) created -> ready (admit); ready -> running (dispatch); running -> blocked (I/O/event wait); blocked -> ready (I/O/event completion); running -> terminated (exit). There is no timer/preemption edge from running to ready. (b)(i) while(TEST-AND-SET(&mutex)); and mutex=0. These printed hyphenated names are pseudocode, not valid C identifiers. (ii) With atomic test-and-set, terminating critical sections and eventual scheduling, the lock is deadlock-free but not starvation-free: one contender may repeatedly lose. (iii) Without atomicity, P reads mutex=0 and is suspended before writing; Q reads 0, writes 1 and enters; P resumes, writes 1 and enters too. Both return their locally read zero, violating mutual exclusion.

questions.text:
A computer uses 32-bit virtual and physical addresses, byte-addressable physical memory, and 4 Kbyte pages. Two-level page tables use equal numbers of index bits at each level. Each page-table entry is 4 bytes.
(a) Give a diagram showing virtual-to-physical translation.
(b) How many page-table entries fit in each page?
(c) How many bits are available for protection and other information in each page-table entry?
questions.referenceAnswer: (a) Split the virtual address as [directory index:10 | table index:10 | offset:12]. The directory base plus 4 times the first index selects a second-level table frame. That table base plus 4 times the second index selects the physical page frame. Concatenate its 20-bit frame number with the unchanged 12-bit offset. (b) $4096/4=1024$ entries per table page. (c) Physical memory has $2^{32}/2^{12}=2^{20}$ frames, requiring 20 frame-number bits; the remaining $32-20=12$ entry bits can hold protection and other metadata.

questions.text:
The following solution to the single-producer single-consumer problem uses semaphores for synchronization.
[CODE]
(a) Complete the dotted parts.
(b) Using another semaphore variable, insert one statement immediately after p1, immediately before p2, immediately after c1 and immediately before c2 so the program works for multiple producers and consumers.
questions.referenceAnswer: Use P for atomic wait and V for signal. (a) p1=P(b_empty), p2=V(b_full), c1=P(b_full), c2=V(b_empty). (b) Introduce a binary semaphore mutex initialized to 1. Insert P(mutex) after p1, V(mutex) before p2, P(mutex) after c1, and V(mutex) before c2. Both buffer-index critical sections share this lock. Wait for space/items BEFORE taking mutex, preventing a full/empty-buffer wait from blocking the counterpart that must make progress. Production and consumption outside the buffer remain outside the lock.

questions.text:
We require a four-state automaton to recognize the regular expression $(a|b)^*abb$.
(a) Give an NFA.
(b) Give a DFA.
questions.referenceAnswer: (a) NFA start q0 loops on a,b; additionally q0 --a--> q1, q1 --b--> q2, q2 --b--> q3; q3 is accepting and has no outgoing transitions. (b) DFA states q0,q1,q2,q3 track longest suffix matching a prefix of abb. On (a,b), transitions are q0:(q1,q0), q1:(q1,q2), q2:(q1,q3), q3:(q1,q0). Start q0; only q3 accepts. Every string is accepted exactly when its suffix is abb.

questions.text:
Answer the following:
(a) Construct all parse trees corresponding to $i+j*k$ for the grammar $E\to E+E$, $E\to E*E$, $E\to\mathrm{di}$.
(b) In this grammar, what is the precedence of * and +?
(c) If only one parse tree is desired for every string in the same language, what changes are needed so the resulting LALR(1) grammar is unambiguous?
questions.referenceAnswer: The scan prints di for the identifier token; interpret it as id, consistent with the identifiers i,j,k in the requested expression. (a) Two trees: E(E(i)+E(E(j)*E(k))) and E(E(E(i)+E(j))*E(k)), representing i+(j*k) and (i+j)*k respectively. Each i,j,k is an id leaf. (b) The ambiguous grammar establishes no unique precedence between * and +. (c) Choose the usual multiplication precedence and left associativity: $E\to E+T\mid T$, $T\to T*F\mid F$, $F\to\mathrm{id}$. This preserves the language of alternating identifiers and the two operators, and gives a unique parse; it is LALR(1). A different explicitly chosen consistent precedence can also satisfy the request.
